concepts.title: Manual Attendance Register Volume
concepts.definition: Marking attendance by hand multiplies fast: one mark per student per working day means the class teacher writes student-count times working-days entries every month, and the school year multiplies that again. The sheer volume explains why pen-and-paper registers invite skipped rows, wrong names and tiring totals.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply students by working days for one month's marks, then by the number of months for the whole session's workload.
question_patterns: a class of 50 students meets 26 days a month; how many attendance marks does the teacher record monthly
how many manual entries pile up over a 10-month session for the 50-student class
why does manual data entry become tedious as data volume grows
list two limitations of maintaining an attendance register by hand
a 40-student class works 24 days; compute the month's entry count
how many marks are written per day for a class of 50 students

solution_steps.explain: every student needs one mark each working day, giving the month's entries
multiplying the monthly load by the number of months gives the session total

worked_examples.q: A class of 40 students meets 24 working days a month. How many attendance entries does the teacher write monthly?

concepts.title: File System Limitations
concepts.definition: Storing school records as separate files brings six recurring troubles: data can be reached only by writing programs, the same facts get duplicated in many files, duplicated copies drift out of agreement, related files have no link between them, programs break when a file's layout changes, and fine-grained read-only access is hard to enforce.
concepts.key_idea: Files alone cannot retrieve, link, de-duplicate or police data; programs must do everything, and they break on format changes.
question_patterns: what are the limitations of file system that a relational DBMS can overcome
define data redundancy with the example of two files holding student names
how does data inconsistency arise when two people maintain two files
what is data isolation in a file system
why does changing a file's structure force changes in application programs
why is controlled data sharing difficult to enforce in a file system

solution_steps.action: ask how the data is reached
solution_steps.explain: files ship no retrieval mechanism; every access needs a bespoke application program
the same student name written in two files is redundancy, and divergent copies are inconsistency
no mapping joins related files, format changes break programs, and per-user access rights are almost unenforceable

worked_examples.q: The same facts stored in many files is called what?

concepts.title: Removing Redundancy by Splitting Tables
concepts.definition: Moving from files to a database trims duplicated storage. Dropping the student-name column from the attendance table removes one copied value from every attendance row, and housing guardian facts once in their own table (reached through a GUID) removes the repeated guardian details for siblings.
concepts.key_idea: Each dropped duplicated column saves one stored value per row; multiplying rows by dropped columns quantifies the saving.
concepts.textbook_ref: keip107.txt section 7.3.1 File System to DBMS (lines 382-449)
question_patterns: why need SName not be maintained in the ATTENDANCE table of the database
1300 monthly attendance rows shrink from 4 columns to 3; how many stored values are saved
how does a separate GUARDIAN table avoid repeating guardian details for siblings
why is a new column GUID needed to identify guardians
why could guardian phone number not serve as the guardian identifier
how does a DBMS avoid redundancy that a file system cannot

solution_steps.action: count the stored values before trimming
solution_steps.explain: multiply the attendance rows by the original wider column count
the same rows now hold one value fewer per row
the difference between the two counts is the duplicated storage removed

worked_examples.q: Dropping the student-name column from a 500-row attendance table removes how many copied values?

concepts.title: Degree and Cardinality of a Relation
concepts.definition: For any relation, the degree is a column count and the cardinality is a row count: GUARDIAN with its four columns and five guardian rows is a degree-4, cardinality-5 relation. Adding one more column raises the degree by one, and the grid of stored values is the degree multiplied by the cardinality.
concepts.key_idea: Columns give the degree, rows give the cardinality, and their product counts every stored value in the relation.
question_patterns: what is the degree of the GUARDIAN relation
what is the cardinality of the GUARDIAN relation shown in the chapter
a relation has 4 attributes and 5 tuples; how many data values does it store
differentiate between degree and cardinality of a relation
if one more column is added to GUARDIAN, what is its new degree
name the terms for the number of attributes and the number of rows of a relation

solution_steps.action: raise the degree for the new column
solution_steps.explain: each added attribute increases the degree by exactly one
the cell count of the relation is its degree times its cardinality

worked_examples.q: A relation has 4 columns and 5 rows. What is its degree?

concepts.title: Attendance Status P and A Tally
concepts.definition: The attendance table stores one letter per student per day, P for present or A for absent. A student's attendance figure for a period is the working days minus the absences, expressed as a percentage of the working days, and roll numbers link each status row back to the STUDENT table.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the A-rows from the working days to get attended days, then scale by 100 for the percentage.
question_patterns: Ali Shah was absent on 2018-09-01 and present on 2018-09-02; find his attendance percentage for the two days
Taleem Shah is marked A on both days in the ATTENDANCE table; what is his attendance percentage
how is the letter A used in the attendance table
which column links the ATTENDANCE table to the STUDENT table
a student attends 24 of 26 working days; compute the attendance percentage
why is the pair of AttendanceDate and RollNumber unique in each attendance record

solution_steps.explain: subtract the absences from the working days of the period
divide the attended days by the working days and scale by 100

worked_examples.q: A student was absent on 6 of 30 working days. What is the attendance percentage?

concepts.title: DBMS Terms: Schema, Instance, Metadata
concepts.definition: A DBMS manages related data through a small vocabulary: the schema is the skeleton design of tables, columns and constraints; the instance is the snapshot of actual contents at a moment; metadata (the data dictionary or catalog) records the schema itself; a query asks for information; and insertion, deletion and update are the three data manipulation operations.
concepts.key_idea: Schema is the design, instance is the current contents, metadata describes the design, queries read, manipulation writes.
question_patterns: differentiate between database state and database schema
what is metadata or the data dictionary of a database
give one example of a query against the student attendance database
name the three data manipulation operations on a database
which operation is needed when a guardian changes his mobile number
what does the database engine do in a DBMS

solution_steps.explain: the schema names tables and constraints; the instance is whatever rows exist right now

solution_steps.action: locate the description of the design
solution_steps.explain: the DBMS stores schema plus constraints as metadata inside its catalog
reading is a query; adding, removing or changing rows is data manipulation

worked_examples.q: What is the skeleton design of tables, columns and constraints called?

concepts.title: Relational Model: Attribute, Tuple, Domain
concepts.definition: In the relational data model a table is a relation: its columns are attributes, each row is a tuple, and every attribute draws values from one domain (its permitted set, usually fixed by a data type). Three properties hold: attribute names are unique and their order is immaterial, tuples are distinct and unordered, and every value is atomic, single-valued and domain-conforming, with NULL marking the unknown.
concepts.key_idea: Columns are named attributes over fixed domains, rows are distinct unordered tuples, and every cell holds one atomic value or NULL.
question_patterns: define attribute, tuple and domain of a relation
which term describes each row of data in a relation
what are the three properties imposed on a relation in the relational model
why must every value of an attribute come from the same domain
what does the special value NULL represent in a column such as GPhone
can two tuples of a relation be identical in all attributes

solution_steps.explain: unique column names are attributes; each attribute has one domain of allowed values
every row is a tuple describing one real-world entity, and no two tuples may be fully identical
each cell carries a single atomic value from the domain, or NULL when the fact is unknown

worked_examples.q: What is a row of a relation called?

concepts.title: Keys: Candidate, Primary, Composite, Foreign
concepts.definition: Keys police uniqueness and relationships. Attributes that never repeat are candidate keys; the designer picks one as the primary key and the rest become alternate keys; when no single attribute suffices, two or more join into a composite primary key such as {RollNumber, AttendanceDate}; and an attribute pointing at another table's primary key is a foreign key, which may stay NULL when it is not part of its own table's key.
concepts.key_idea: Candidate keys are the options, the chosen one is primary, leftovers are alternate, combined ones are composite, and cross-table pointers are foreign.
question_patterns: name the candidate keys of the GUARDIAN relation
if GUID is chosen as primary key of GUARDIAN, what is GPhone called
why must ATTENDANCE use a composite primary key of RollNumber and AttendanceDate
which attribute acts as a foreign key in the STUDENT relation
why are foreign keys allowed to hold NULL values
can roll number 17 appear twice in a sports preference table where Roll_no is the primary key

solution_steps.explain: any attribute whose values never repeat and are never NULL is a candidate key
one candidate becomes the primary key; the unchosen candidates are alternate keys
when one attribute cannot separate tuples, several join as a composite key; an attribute referencing another relation's primary key is a foreign key

worked_examples.q: RollNumber together with AttendanceDate forms which kind of key?

worked_examples.question_pattern: Class strength is 50 and a month has 26 working days. How many attendance marks are recorded manually in the month, and how many over a 10-month session?
The attendance table holds 1300 rows for the month. Dropping the SName column reduces it from 4 columns to 3. How many stored values are saved?

questions: Give the terms: collection of logically related records (database/relations); DBMS file describing stored data (metadata); attribute that uniquely identifies tuples (candidate key); special value for unknown data (NULL); unique identifier not chosen as primary key (alternate key); software to create and maintain a relational database (DBMS).
Differentiate between primary key and foreign key with the STUDENT-ATTENDANCE example.
In the Sports Preferences table, roll no 17 lists two preferences. Which property of a relation is violated? (each cell must be atomic/single-valued)
In the same table, can roll no 24's preference be NULL when the school rule says every student must participate? (no, a rule constraint forbids it)
Kabaddi was chosen by nobody; can such a tuple exist in the relation? (the given table shape stores student preferences, so a tuple without a student violates the design)
Are two sports preference tables equivalent when one is sorted by roll number and the other by sports name? (yes, tuple order is immaterial in a relation)
